[PATH:empirical] Azar, J., Marinescu, I., & Steinbaum, M. (2022). Labor market concentration and minimum wage effects. Journal of Labor Economics, 40(S1), S167-S200. — This paper directly examines how employer concentration moderates the employment and earnings effects of minimum wage increases, providing a baseline empirical test of the hypothesis across different product demand conditions.

[PATH:empirical] Berger, D., Herkenhoff, K., & Mongey, S. (2022). Minimum wages, market power, and product market elasticities. American Economic Review, 112(4), 1218-1259. — This study explicitly models how product demand elasticity interacts with labor market concentration to determine the net earnings effects of minimum wage changes, offering direct evidence for or against the conditional amplification hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Robinson, J. (1933). The Economics of Imperfect Competition. London: Macmillan. — This foundational text provides the theoretical framework for monopsony power and its interaction with product demand elasticity, which is essential for deriving testable predictions about when minimum wage increases lead to net gains versus losses for low-skilled workers.

scope.domain: high employer concentration labor markets with varying product demand elasticity

[PATH:empirical] Azar, J., Marinescu, I., & Steinbaum, M. (2022). Labor market concentration. Journal of Human Resources, 57(S), S167-S199. — Provides direct empirical estimates of employer concentration across U.S. labor markets and its effects on wages and employment, which can be used to test whether concentrated markets dampen the earnings gains from minimum wage increases.

[PATH:empirical] Cengiz, D., Dube, A., Lindner, A., & Zipperer, B. (2019). The effect of minimum wages on low-wage jobs. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 134(3), 1405-1454. — Examines minimum wage impacts on job availability and unemployment using a border discontinuity design; re-analyzing these data by local employer concentration levels can confirm or refute whether concentration moderates net earnings gains.

[PATH:theoretical] Manning, A. (2021). Monopsony in labor markets: A review. ILR Review, 74(1), 3-26. — Provides a theoretical framework linking employer concentration (monopsony power) to minimum wage effects on employment and earnings, offering predictions that can be tested against empirical findings in high-concentration settings.

[PATH:empirical] Azar, J., Marinescu, I., & Steinbaum, M. (2022). Labor market concentration and the wage effects of minimum wages. Journal of Human Resources, 57(S), S113-S142. — This study directly examines how local labor market concentration moderates the wage and employment effects of minimum wage increases, providing empirical evidence on whether concentrated markets dampen earnings gains and reduce hours more sharply.

[PATH:theoretical] Berger, D., Herkenhoff, K., & Mongey, S. (2022). Minimum wages, employment, and the market power of firms. NBER Working Paper No. 29812. — This theoretical paper models how employer market power interacts with minimum wage policies, predicting differential employment and hours responses in concentrated versus competitive markets, which can be tested against the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Dube, A., Lester, T. W., & Reich, M. (2016). Minimum wage shocks, employment flows, and labor market frictions. Journal of Labor Economics, 34(3), 663-704. — While not focused on concentration, this paper provides robust empirical methods for estimating employment and hours effects of minimum wages; re-analyzing their data with local concentration measures could confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing minimum wage studies (e.g., from the Journal of Labor Economics, 2000–2023) that explicitly code for employer concentration or market competitiveness, to assess whether low-concentration contexts consistently amplify positive earnings effects. — Synthesizes evidence across multiple studies to determine if the hypothesized relationship is robust or an artifact of specific datasets or methods.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of search-and-bargaining frameworks (e.g., Manning's monopsony models) calibrated to low-concentration US labor markets, simulating minimum wage impacts on earnings and employment. — Provides a causal mechanism for the hypothesis by showing how reduced employer market power in low-concentration settings can increase workers' bargaining leverage, leading to higher net earnings gains from wage floors.
